stem:
A 3-year-old girl is reviewed on the paediatric ward five days after an episode of bloody diarrhoea caused by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. She now looks pale, has passed little urine today and has a few petechiae on her legs.

Which set of blood findings would confirm the suspected complication?

options.A: Polycythaemia, raised platelets and a normal creatinine
options.B: Neutropenia, high calcium and a normal creatinine
options.C: Low glucose, high potassium and normal platelets
options.D: Raised white cell count, normal haemoglobin and normal platelets
options.E: Haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells, low platelets and rising creatinine

correct_answer: E. Haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells, low platelets and rising creatinine
why_correct: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Her pallor, petechiae and reduced urine output match each component. A blood film showing schistocytes supports the diagnosis, and management is supportive, sometimes including dialysis.
why_wrong: A. Polycythaemia and thrombocytosis are the opposite of HUS findings. B. Neutropenia and hypercalcaemia are not features of HUS. C. Platelets are low in HUS, and this pattern does not fit. D. HUS causes anaemia and thrombocytopenia, so normal values exclude it.
pearl: In HUS the clotting screen is usually normal, which helps distinguish it from disseminated intravascular coagulation.
thinking: Recent STEC diarrhoea ↓ Pallor suggests anaemia ↓ Petechiae suggest low platelets ↓ Reduced urine output suggests kidney injury ↓ Triad confirms haemolytic uraemic syndrome
exam_trap: C, Low glucose, high potassium and normal platelets — hyperkalaemia can occur with kidney injury, but normal platelets rule out HUS.
takeaway: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is the triad of haemolytic anaemia, low platelets and acute kidney injury.

stem:
A 38-year-old man who moved from Pakistan last year walks into a busy emergency department. He has coughed for two months, has lost weight and wakes drenched in sweat. The triage nurse suspects pulmonary tuberculosis.

What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Place him in a single room with airborne precautions and collect sputum for acid-fast bacilli
options.B: Ask him to wait in the main waiting area until a chest X-ray is done
options.C: Start four-drug TB treatment before sending any samples
options.D: Give a week of amoxicillin and review if the cough continues
options.E: Send an interferon-gamma release assay and discharge him home

correct_answer: A. Place him in a single room with airborne precautions and collect sputum for acid-fast bacilli
why_correct: His prolonged cough, weight loss and night sweats make infectious pulmonary TB likely. He should be separated from others in a single room with airborne precautions to prevent spread. Several sputum samples should be sent for smear, culture and rapid molecular testing so the diagnosis and drug sensitivities can be confirmed before treatment.
why_wrong: B. Sitting in a crowded waiting area risks airborne spread to other patients. C. Starting treatment before sampling reduces the chance of confirming the diagnosis and sensitivities. D. Amoxicillin does not treat TB and delays diagnosis. E. An interferon-gamma release assay cannot diagnose active disease, and discharge risks transmission.
pearl: In suspected pulmonary TB, at least three sputum samples are sent, including one early-morning sample if possible.
thinking: Prolonged cough, weight loss and night sweats ↓ Possible infectious TB ↓ Protect others first with airborne isolation ↓ Obtain sputum before treatment ↓ Confirm diagnosis and sensitivities
exam_trap: C, Start four-drug TB treatment before sending any samples — treating quickly feels safe, but without samples the diagnosis and drug resistance cannot be confirmed.
takeaway: Suspected pulmonary TB needs airborne isolation and sputum samples before treatment starts.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman who works in a homeless shelter sees her GP with three months of cough, sweats at night and a drop in dress size. Her chest X-ray shows a cavity in the right apex.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A subacute illness with cough, night sweats and weight loss together with an apical cavity is the classic picture of reactivation pulmonary TB. Working in a homeless shelter is an additional exposure risk. She needs isolation advice, sputum testing and urgent referral to the TB service.
why_wrong: B. Asthma causes episodic wheeze and does not produce cavities. C. Pneumothorax presents suddenly with pleuritic pain and breathlessness. D. Pulmonary oedema causes bilateral shadowing and breathlessness, not apical cavitation. E. Pneumonia is usually acute and causes consolidation rather than an apical cavity.
pearl: TB favours the lung apices because of their high oxygen tension.
thinking: Three months of cough ↓ Night sweats and weight loss ↓ Exposure risk at work ↓ Apical cavity on X-ray ↓ Pulmonary tuberculosis
exam_trap: E, Community-acquired pneumonia — cough and sweats suggest infection, but a three-month course and an apical cavity point to TB.
takeaway: Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and an apical cavity indicate pulmonary TB.

stem:
A practice nurse is reviewing new patient registration questionnaires from people recently arrived from countries with high TB rates. She asks the GP which reported set of symptoms should most prompt assessment for active pulmonary tuberculosis.

Which is it?

options.A: Wheeze and chest tightness at night that comes and goes
options.B: A cough lasting several weeks with weight loss and night sweats
options.C: Sudden fever, productive cough and sharp chest pain for two days
options.E: Sudden loss of vision in one eye

correct_answer: B. A cough lasting several weeks with weight loss and night sweats
why_correct: A persistent cough lasting more than a few weeks combined with systemic symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats is the classic presentation of active pulmonary TB. These features should prompt a chest X-ray and sputum testing. Recent migration from a high-incidence country increases the likelihood.
why_wrong: A. Variable nocturnal wheeze and chest tightness suggests asthma. C. A short history of fever, productive cough and pleuritic pain suggests pneumonia. D. Dysuria and frequency suggest a urinary tract infection. E. Sudden monocular visual loss suggests a vascular or retinal problem.
pearl: Haemoptysis, fever and loss of appetite are other features that raise suspicion of pulmonary TB.
thinking: Screening people from high-incidence countries ↓ TB is a slowly progressive infection ↓ Look for persistent cough ↓ Plus systemic symptoms ↓ Weight loss and night sweats
exam_trap: C, Sudden fever, productive cough and sharp chest pain for two days — fever and cough suggest a chest infection, but the short history fits acute pneumonia rather than TB.
takeaway: Weeks of cough with weight loss and night sweats should prompt assessment for TB.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman is told at the sexual health clinic that she has HIV. Her CD4 count is in the normal range and she has no symptoms. She would prefer to wait until she feels unwell before starting any medicines.

What is the main reason treatment is advised now?

options.A: HIV is usually cleared by the immune system, so treatment is short
options.B: Treatment is only needed when an opportunistic infection develops
options.C: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus, protects the immune system and prevents progression
options.D: Treatment is delayed until the CD4 count falls below a set level
options.E: A short antiretroviral course will eradicate the virus completely

correct_answer: C. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus, protects the immune system and prevents progression
why_correct: Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for everyone diagnosed with HIV, whatever the CD4 count, because suppressing viral replication preserves immune function and reduces illness and death. Starting early is better than waiting for symptoms. An undetectable viral load also prevents sexual transmission to partners.
why_wrong: A. HIV is not cleared spontaneously. B. Waiting for an opportunistic infection means significant immune damage has already occurred. D. Treatment is no longer delayed until the CD4 count falls. E. Treatment controls but does not eradicate HIV, so it is lifelong.
pearl: Undetectable equals untransmittable: a person with a sustained undetectable viral load does not pass HIV on sexually.
thinking: New HIV diagnosis ↓ Asymptomatic with normal CD4 count ↓ Guidance advises treatment for all ↓ Viral suppression preserves immunity ↓ Lifelong therapy prevents progression
exam_trap: D, Treatment is delayed until the CD4 count falls below a set level — this was past practice, but current guidance recommends starting regardless of CD4 count.
takeaway: Everyone with HIV is offered antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis, regardless of symptoms or CD4 count.

presentation: Long-term effects of chronic hepatitis B
stem: A 40-year-old man who grew up in West Africa is tested after his pregnant partner is found to have hepatitis B on antenatal screening. His results show long-standing chronic hepatitis B infection. He feels well and asks the GP which part of his body the infection is most likely to damage over time.
why_correct: Hepatitis B is a hepatotropic virus, and chronic infection causes ongoing liver inflammation. Over years this can lead to fibrosis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, sometimes even without cirrhosis. He should be referred to a hepatology service for assessment and surveillance.
why_wrong: A. Kidney involvement, such as membranous nephropathy, can occur but is uncommon. B. The bone marrow is not the main target of hepatitis B. C. The heart is not a typical site of hepatitis B damage. D. The thyroid is not affected by hepatitis B.
pearl: Unlike most causes of liver cancer, chronic hepatitis B can lead to hepatocellular carcinoma without cirrhosis being present.
thinking: Chronic hepatitis B carrier ↓ Hepatitis B targets hepatocytes ↓ Persistent inflammation ↓ Fibrosis and cirrhosis ↓ Risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
exam_trap: A, Kidneys — hepatitis B-associated glomerulonephritis is a recognised extrahepatic feature, but it is far less common than liver disease.
takeaway: The main long-term target of chronic hepatitis B is the liver, leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
notes: Reviewer fix: Implausible stem ('found on antenatal screening of his partner's family') reworded to partner-positive antenatal screen prompting his test.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the ED by his wife. Over two days he has developed a temperature and has been saying odd things and acting out of character. In the department he has a seizure starting in his right arm.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever with altered behaviour, confusion and a focal seizure indicates inflammation of the brain tissue itself, typical of encephalitis. Herpes simplex virus is the commonest identifiable cause in the UK. Intravenous aciclovir should be started promptly while MRI and lumbar puncture are arranged.
why_wrong: A. Tension-type headache does not cause fever, confusion or seizures. B. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness without encephalopathy. C. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo only. E. Migraine without aura does not cause fever, personality change or seizures.
pearl: Delay in starting aciclovir in herpes simplex encephalitis is linked with worse outcomes, so treatment should not wait for test results.
thinking: Fever ↓ Behavioural change and confusion ↓ Focal seizure ↓ Brain parenchyma is involved ↓ Suspect encephalitis
exam_trap: E, Migraine without aura — headache and odd behaviour may suggest migraine, but fever and a focal seizure are never explained by it.
takeaway: Fever with confusion, behavioural change and seizures should be treated as encephalitis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman is admitted by the medical team after her flatmate found her disorientated and feverish. She has been unusually aggressive for a day and has had two fits. MRI shows abnormal signal in the temporal lobes.

Which virus is the most important cause to consider?
why_correct: Herpes simplex virus is the commonest identified cause of sporadic viral encephalitis in the UK. It has a predilection for the temporal lobes, producing personality change, confusion and seizures. Intravenous aciclovir should be started immediately and CSF sent for HSV PCR.
why_wrong: A. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis in young children. C. HPV causes warts and genital cancers, not encephalitis. D. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis. E. Norovirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
pearl: Temporal lobe involvement on MRI or EEG is a strong pointer towards herpes simplex encephalitis.
thinking: Fever and confusion ↓ Behavioural change and seizures ↓ Temporal lobe changes on MRI ↓ Commonest viral cause is HSV ↓ Start IV aciclovir
exam_trap: E, Norovirus — it is a very common virus that can cause febrile illness in adults, but it causes gastroenteritis, not brain infection.
takeaway: Herpes simplex virus is the key viral cause of encephalitis, especially with temporal lobe changes.

stem:
A 4-month-old boy who was born in another country is seen by the paediatric team. He failed his hearing tests, has a heart murmur from a patent ductus arteriosus and has bilateral cataracts. His mother remembers having a rash and swollen neck glands in the first weeks of pregnancy.

Which maternal infection is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Rubella in the first trimester can cross the placenta and cause congenital rubella syndrome. The classic features are sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease such as patent ductus arteriosus, and eye defects including cataracts. The risk of defects is highest when infection occurs early in pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Influenza does not cause this pattern of congenital defects. B. Hepatitis A is not associated with congenital malformations. C. A urinary infection does not cause congenital deafness or cataracts. D. Tonsillitis does not cross the placenta to cause fetal defects.
pearl: Rubella is prevented by MMR vaccination; MMR is a live vaccine, so it is not given during pregnancy and pregnancy should be avoided for one month afterwards.
thinking: Deafness ↓ Patent ductus arteriosus ↓ Cataracts ↓ Maternal rash early in pregnancy ↓ Congenital rubella syndrome
exam_trap: A, Influenza — a febrile illness in early pregnancy can seem relevant, but influenza does not cause the deafness, heart and eye triad.
takeaway: Sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease and cataracts point to congenital rubella.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. The TB nurse is planning contact tracing.

Who among the people she has had contact with is the highest priority for assessment?

options.A: A colleague who works on a different floor of her office
options.B: Her sister, who lives in another city and visited once last year
options.C: A pharmacist who dispensed her prescription
options.D: Her 2-year-old grandson, who lives with her
options.E: A neighbour she chats to over the fence once a month

correct_answer: D. Her 2-year-old grandson, who lives with her
why_correct: Household contacts have the most prolonged, close exposure to infectious TB and are assessed first. Young children are at particular risk of infection progressing to active disease, including severe forms such as TB meningitis. Her grandson should be assessed promptly by the paediatric TB service.
why_wrong: A. Working on a different floor involves little shared air space. B. A single visit a year ago is minimal exposure. C. A brief transaction at a pharmacy counter is low risk. E. Occasional outdoor conversations carry little risk.
pearl: Children under 5 who are close contacts of infectious TB may be offered preventive treatment even before infection is confirmed.
thinking: Infectious smear-positive TB ↓ Risk depends on how close and long the contact is ↓ Household contacts are highest risk ↓ Young children progress more readily ↓ Prioritise the grandson
exam_trap: A, A colleague who works on a different floor of her office — workplace contacts are often screened, but separate floors mean far less exposure than shared household air.
takeaway: In TB contact tracing, close household contacts, especially young children, are assessed first.

stem:
A 19-year-old university fresher sees the practice nurse. She is starting a new relationship and wants to avoid pregnancy, but she also wants to lower her chance of catching chlamydia or other infections.

Which method meets both aims?
why_correct: Barrier methods such as male and female condoms are the only contraceptives that also reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted infections. She can use condoms alone or alongside a more reliable hormonal or intrauterine method for extra pregnancy protection. Free condoms are available from sexual health services.
why_wrong: A. The progestogen-only pill prevents pregnancy but gives no STI protection. B. The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but does not protect against infection. C. The combined pill does not prevent STIs. E. The injection does not protect against STIs.
pearl: Using condoms together with a long-acting reversible method is sometimes called double Dutch and gives highly effective protection against both pregnancy and STIs.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Also wants infection protection ↓ Hormonal and intrauterine methods do not protect ↓ Barrier blocks fluid exchange ↓ Condoms
exam_trap: B, Copper intrauterine device — it is among the most effective contraceptives, which tempts, but it offers no protection against STIs.
takeaway: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman attends the infectious diseases clinic. She was found to have HIV two years ago but stopped antiretroviral therapy last year, and her CD4 count is now very low. Sputum culture has grown Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The registrar explains to the foundation doctor why this pairing of infections matters.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Tuberculosis in people with HIV is usually confined to the lungs
options.B: Sputum smears are more likely to be positive as immunosuppression advances
options.C: HIV-related immunosuppression greatly raises the risk of latent infection progressing to active tuberculosis
options.D: Antiretroviral therapy should be withheld until the full course of tuberculosis treatment is finished
options.E: Contact tracing is unnecessary because co-infected patients cannot transmit tuberculosis

correct_answer: C. HIV-related immunosuppression greatly raises the risk of latent infection progressing to active tuberculosis
why_correct: Loss of CD4 cell-mediated immunity removes the main defence that keeps Mycobacterium tuberculosis contained in granulomas, so people with HIV are many times more likely to develop active disease, either from reactivation of latent infection or rapid progression of new infection. Disease is also more often extrapulmonary or disseminated. This is why everyone with tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and why co-infected patients need joint specialist care.
why_wrong: A. Extrapulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis become more common, not less, as the CD4 count falls. B. Advanced HIV produces fewer cavities, so smear-negative disease is more frequent. D. Antiretroviral therapy is started during tuberculosis treatment, usually within the first weeks, because it improves survival. E. Pulmonary disease in co-infected patients can still be infectious, so contacts must be assessed.
pearl: Everyone diagnosed with active tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and everyone with newly diagnosed HIV should be assessed for tuberculosis.
thinking: HIV with very low CD4 count ↓ Cell-mediated immunity fails to contain mycobacteria ↓ Latent infection reactivates or new infection progresses quickly ↓ More active and extrapulmonary tuberculosis ↓ HIV greatly increases tuberculosis risk
exam_trap: D, Withholding antiretroviral therapy — concern about drug interactions and immune reconstitution makes delay seem sensible, but antiretrovirals are started during tuberculosis treatment because waiting increases mortality.
takeaway: HIV markedly increases the risk of developing active, often extrapulmonary, tuberculosis.

stem:
A 47-year-old man who sleeps in a homeless hostel is brought to the emergency department after coughing up streaks of blood. He has been unwell for two months and his clothes now hang loosely on him. His chest radiograph shows a cavitating lesion in the right upper lobe. The acute medical unit has a bed available in a six-bedded bay.

What should happen first?

options.A: Admit him to the open bay with standard precautions while sputum results are awaited
options.B: Give a first dose of quadruple antituberculous therapy and discharge him back to the hostel
options.C: Repeat the chest radiograph after a course of antibiotics before deciding on further action
options.D: Place him in a single room with airborne precautions and refer urgently to the tuberculosis team
options.E: Start oral amoxicillin for community-acquired pneumonia and review in the clinic

correct_answer: D. Place him in a single room with airborne precautions and refer urgently to the tuberculosis team
why_correct: Haemoptysis, prolonged illness with weight loss, a high-risk social background and upper lobe cavitation make infectious pulmonary tuberculosis likely. The priority is to stop onward spread by isolating him in a single room with airborne precautions (a negative-pressure room if multidrug-resistant disease is suspected), then to involve the tuberculosis service for sputum samples and specialist assessment before treatment starts.
why_wrong: A. An open bay exposes other, possibly vulnerable, patients to airborne infection. B. Treatment should follow sputum sampling and specialist assessment, and discharging a probable infectious case to a hostel risks an outbreak. C. Waiting for repeat imaging delays diagnosis and isolation. E. Treating as simple pneumonia ignores the clear features of tuberculosis.
pearl: Cavitating pulmonary tuberculosis is the most infectious form; at least three sputum samples, including one early morning sample, should be sent for microscopy, culture and rapid molecular testing.
thinking: Haemoptysis and weight loss over months ↓ Hostel resident, a high-risk group ↓ Upper lobe cavity on radiograph ↓ Probable infectious tuberculosis ↓ Isolate with airborne precautions and refer to the tuberculosis team
exam_trap: B, Starting quadruple therapy and discharging — giving treatment feels proactive, but it skips microbiological confirmation and sends a likely infectious patient back into crowded accommodation.
takeaway: Suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis needs immediate airborne isolation and early specialist assessment.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: removed blanket 'ideally negative pressure + staff FFP3' (NICE NG33 reserves negative pressure/FFP3 for suspected MDR or AGPs); now single room with airborne precautions, negative pressure if MDR suspected

stem:
A mother phones NHS 111 in the evening. Since yesterday she, her husband and their two school-age children have all had sudden vomiting and loose watery stools. Nobody has blood in the stool, all are drinking, and none had bowel problems before this week.

Which diagnosis best explains the situation?
why_correct: Abrupt vomiting and watery stools affecting a whole family within a day or two points to a transmissible infection, most often viral, spread person to person or through shared food. Chronic bowel conditions develop over weeks to months in one individual and would not appear simultaneously in four people.
why_wrong: B. Ulcerative colitis causes chronic bloody diarrhoea in one person, not a family cluster. C. Irritable bowel syndrome is a long-standing functional disorder and does not start suddenly in several relatives. D. Coeliac disease causes gradual symptoms after gluten exposure, not an acute shared illness. E. Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory condition with a subacute course.
pearl: Children with gastroenteritis should stay off school or nursery until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Vomiting plus watery diarrhoea ↓ Several family members affected at once ↓ No prior bowel history ↓ Transmissible infective gastroenteritis
exam_trap: C, Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea — it is a very common cause of loose stools, but it is chronic and cannot explain a sudden illness shared by a household.
takeaway: An acute cluster of vomiting and diarrhoea in one household is infective gastroenteritis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with two days of fever, griping lower abdominal pain and frequent loose stools. Three days ago he ate a homemade dessert made with raw eggs at a family party, and his sister who ate the same dessert is also unwell.

Which bacterium is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea starting a day or so after eating raw or undercooked egg is a classic picture of non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis. A second case linked to the same food supports a foodborne source. Most cases settle with fluids alone, and suspected food poisoning is notifiable to UKHSA.
why_wrong: A. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough, not foodborne diarrhoea. B. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis. D. Clostridium tetani causes tetanus with muscle spasm. E. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease after a tick bite.
pearl: Antibiotics are not usually needed for non-typhoidal Salmonella and may prolong carriage; they are reserved for severe illness, the very young or old, and the immunocompromised.
thinking: Fever, cramps and diarrhoea ↓ Onset about a day after raw egg dessert ↓ Another person who ate it is unwell ↓ Foodborne bacterial gastroenteritis ↓ Salmonella
exam_trap: D, Clostridium tetani — the 'Clostridium' name suggests the diarrhoea-causing C. difficile, but C. tetani causes tetanus and has no role in food poisoning.
takeaway: Raw or undercooked egg followed by febrile diarrhoea suggests Salmonella.

stem:
A 21-year-old woman attends the walk-in centre with three days of fever, colicky central abdominal pain and diarrhoea that today contained a little blood. The illness began four days after a barbecue where the chicken was pink in the middle.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Campylobacter is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK and is strongly linked to undercooked poultry. It has an incubation period of a few days and causes fever, marked cramping abdominal pain and diarrhoea that may become bloody. The timing and food history here fit it well.
why_wrong: A. Bacillus cereus causes vomiting or diarrhoea within hours of eating reheated rice, not days later. B. Staphylococcus aureus toxin causes sudden vomiting within a few hours of eating. C. Cholera causes profuse painless watery stools after travel to endemic areas. E. Giardia causes prolonged, non-bloody, malabsorptive diarrhoea after drinking untreated water.
pearl: Campylobacter infection is the most common antecedent of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
thinking: Undercooked chicken ↓ Symptoms start several days later ↓ Fever, cramps and diarrhoea with some blood ↓ Commonest UK bacterial enteric pathogen from poultry ↓ Campylobacter
exam_trap: B, Staphylococcus aureus — it is a well-known cause of food poisoning, but its preformed toxin causes vomiting within hours, which does not match a several-day incubation.
takeaway: Undercooked poultry followed days later by febrile, sometimes bloody, diarrhoea suggests Campylobacter.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman who was treated in hospital for Clostridioides difficile infection last winter asks her GP for antibiotics for a cough and sore throat that look viral. The GP advises against them and she asks how antibiotics led to her bowel infection.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Antibiotics directly ulcerate the colonic lining, which then becomes infected
options.B: Antibiotics suppress the normal colonic bacteria, allowing C. difficile to multiply and release toxins
options.C: Antibiotics trigger an allergic reaction in the colon that mimics infection
options.D: Antibiotics carry C. difficile spores into the bowel from the tablet coating
options.E: Antibiotics make C. difficile invade the bloodstream and seed the colon

correct_answer: B. Antibiotics suppress the normal colonic bacteria, allowing C. difficile to multiply and release toxins
why_correct: The healthy colonic microbiota resists colonisation by C. difficile. Antibiotics, especially broad-spectrum agents, disrupt this flora, so ingested spores can germinate, multiply and release toxins A and B that damage the colon. Avoiding antibiotics that are not needed is therefore a key part of preventing first and recurrent episodes.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not ulcerate the colon directly; the damage comes from C. difficile toxins. C. The colitis is toxin-mediated infection, not an allergic reaction. D. Spores are acquired from the environment or contacts, not from medicines. E. C. difficile is a non-invasive luminal pathogen and does not spread through the blood.
pearl: Clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and fluoroquinolones carry the highest risk, and proton pump inhibitors add to it.
thinking: Previous C. difficile infection ↓ Antibiotics disturb protective gut flora ↓ Spores germinate and multiply ↓ Toxins injure the colon ↓ Avoid unnecessary antibiotics to prevent recurrence
exam_trap: A, Direct ulceration by antibiotics — it sounds like a plausible drug side effect, but the injury comes from bacterial toxins after the protective flora is lost.
takeaway: Antibiotics cause C. difficile infection by wiping out the normal flora that keeps it in check.

stem:
On a care of the elderly ward, an 83-year-old man has had five loose, foul-smelling stools since this morning. Two other patients in his bay developed diarrhoea over the past week and C. difficile toxin results are pending.

Which infection-control measure is most appropriate?

options.A: Give oral vancomycin to the other patients in the bay as prophylaxis
options.B: Keep him in the bay and rely on alcohol hand rub between patients
options.C: Clean the bay with standard detergent and wait for the toxin result before acting
options.D: Encourage him to use the shared bay toilet so that his stool output can be observed
options.E: Move him to a single room with contact precautions, soap and water hand washing and chlorine-based cleaning

correct_answer: E. Move him to a single room with contact precautions, soap and water hand washing and chlorine-based cleaning
why_correct: Possible infectious diarrhoea should be isolated at once, without waiting for results, particularly when a cluster suggests ward transmission. C. difficile forms spores that survive on surfaces and resist alcohol, so staff need gloves and aprons, must wash hands with soap and water, and the environment must be cleaned with a chlorine-releasing or other sporicidal agent.
why_wrong: A. Prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic contacts is not recommended. B. Alcohol hand rub does not kill spores and the patient stays among others. C. Detergent alone does not remove spores, and delaying action allows further spread. D. Shared toilets spread spores; he needs his own toilet or commode.
pearl: Isolate any patient with diarrhoea that could be infective within two hours, and treat two or more linked cases on a ward as a possible outbreak needing the infection prevention and control team.
thinking: New diarrhoea in an inpatient ↓ Cluster in the same bay ↓ Suspect C. difficile before results return ↓ Spores resist alcohol and detergent ↓ Single room, contact precautions, soap and water, sporicidal cleaning
exam_trap: B, Relying on alcohol hand rub — it is the usual default for hand hygiene on wards, but it does not kill C. difficile spores, so soap and water is needed.
takeaway: Suspected C. difficile requires prompt isolation, soap and water hand washing and sporicidal environmental cleaning.

stem:
A 45-year-old aid worker is assessed in the emergency department the day after flying back from a flood-hit area where clean water was scarce. Since the night before he has passed large volumes of painless, pale watery stools with flecks of mucus, like the water rice has been cooked in. He has little fever but feels faint on standing.

Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden, massive, painless watery stools with a rice-water appearance after exposure to contaminated water in a disaster setting is the classic picture of cholera. The enterotoxin drives large secretory losses of water and salt with little inflammation, so fever is minimal but hypovolaemia develops quickly. Urgent rehydration is the priority.
why_wrong: A. Shigella causes dysentery with fever, cramps and blood or mucus in small frequent stools. B. Giardia causes a gradual, prolonged, bloating and greasy diarrhoea. D. Campylobacter causes painful, febrile, often bloody diarrhoea. E. Salmonella usually causes febrile gastroenteritis with cramps rather than massive painless losses.
pearl: Cholera is a notifiable disease in the UK, and most deaths are prevented by prompt oral rehydration solution or intravenous fluids rather than antibiotics.
thinking: Recent stay in an area without clean water ↓ Sudden painless high-volume stools ↓ Rice-water appearance, little fever ↓ Secretory toxin-mediated diarrhoea ↓ Vibrio cholerae
exam_trap: A, Shigella — it is linked to poor sanitation too, but it causes painful, febrile dysentery with blood, not painless rice-water stools.
takeaway: Painless rice-water diarrhoea with rapid dehydration after contaminated water exposure suggests cholera.

stem:
Over two weeks, several children and parents who used the same leisure centre swimming pool present to local GPs with watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and stomach cramps. A 34-year-old father among them has had symptoms for nine days. UKHSA notes that the parasite involved is resistant to routine pool chlorination.

Which protozoan is most likely?
why_correct: Cryptosporidium is a protozoan whose oocysts resist chlorine, so it is the classic cause of outbreaks linked to swimming pools and water supplies. It causes watery diarrhoea and cramps that usually resolve within two to three weeks in immunocompetent people. Diagnosis is by stool testing (antigen, PCR or microscopy) for Cryptosporidium, and linked cases are investigated by the local health protection team.
why_wrong: A. Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery with bloody stools, usually acquired abroad. B. Plasmodium falciparum causes malaria, transmitted by mosquitoes. C. Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat and usually causes a glandular fever-like illness or congenital infection. E. Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted protozoan causing vaginal discharge.
pearl: In people with advanced HIV, cryptosporidiosis can cause chronic, severe watery diarrhoea and wasting.
thinking: Cluster linked to one swimming pool ↓ Watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with cramps ↓ Organism survives chlorination ↓ Protozoan with resistant oocysts ↓ Cryptosporidium
exam_trap: A, Entamoeba histolytica — it is the best-known gut protozoan, but it causes bloody dysentery and is not the typical chlorine-resistant pool outbreak organism.
takeaway: Watery diarrhoea outbreaks linked to swimming pools are classically due to Cryptosporidium.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: replaced unsupported claim that Cryptosporidium testing must be specially requested with neutral diagnosis/health protection statement

stem:
A 63-year-old man attends A&E with two days of frequent, high-volume watery stools that started on the last day of a holiday in South Asia. He feels light-headed, his mouth and tongue are dry, and he has passed very little urine today. There is no blood in the stool.

Which complication needs addressing most urgently?
why_correct: Large-volume watery diarrhoea with light-headedness, dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output shows significant fluid and electrolyte loss. Hypovolaemia can progress to acute kidney injury and shock, so assessing severity and replacing fluid is the immediate priority. Older adults are especially vulnerable.
why_wrong: A. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, mainly in children. B. Toxic megacolon complicates severe colitis with abdominal distension and systemic toxicity. C. Reactive arthritis appears weeks after enteric infection, not acutely. D. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a later neurological complication, typically after Campylobacter.
pearl: Check urea, creatinine and electrolytes in significant dehydration, as diarrhoea causes loss of sodium, potassium and bicarbonate.
thinking: High-volume watery diarrhoea ↓ Light-headedness and dry mouth ↓ Reduced urine output ↓ Signs of fluid depletion ↓ Dehydration is the immediate threat
exam_trap: A, Haemolytic uraemic syndrome — reduced urine output hints at the kidneys, but HUS follows bloody diarrhoea, whereas here the oliguria reflects simple fluid loss.
takeaway: The most urgent complication of profuse watery diarrhoea is dehydration.

stem:
In January, a nurse at a residential care home calls the GP practice. Over 36 hours, eight residents and three staff have suddenly developed nausea, forceful vomiting and watery diarrhoea. The first people affected are already improving.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Abrupt vomiting and diarrhoea spreading rapidly among both residents and staff in a closed setting during winter, with recovery in a day or two, is typical of norovirus. It is highly infectious, needs only a tiny dose and survives on surfaces, so the home should close affected areas to admissions, exclude unwell staff until 48 hours symptom-free and contact the local health protection team.
why_wrong: A. C. difficile mainly affects residents after antibiotics, rarely causes prominent vomiting and does not usually affect healthy staff. C. Giardia causes prolonged bloating diarrhoea after untreated water, not explosive short outbreaks. D. Cholera is linked to contaminated water in endemic areas and causes profuse painless stools. E. Shigella causes dysentery with fever and bloody stools.
pearl: Alcohol hand rub is unreliable against norovirus, so soap and water hand washing should be used during outbreaks.
thinking: Closed setting in winter ↓ Sudden vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Rapid spread to residents and staff ↓ Short illness lasting one to two days ↓ Norovirus
exam_trap: A, Clostridioides difficile — it is the familiar cause of diarrhoea in older people in care, but it rarely causes vomiting-led outbreaks that also strike healthy staff.
takeaway: Sudden vomiting and diarrhoea outbreaks in care homes in winter are usually due to norovirus.

stem:
Twenty pupils and two teachers fall ill with vomiting and watery diarrhoea during a school camping trip. The toilet block had no soap, and the same tap was used for drinking and washing up. The environmental health officer asks the visiting doctor how the infection most likely spread.

Which route is most likely?
why_correct: Outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea are usually caused by organisms passed from faeces to the mouth through contaminated hands, food or water. Missing soap and a shared tap for drinking and washing up provide exactly these routes. Hand hygiene with soap and water and safe food and water handling are the key control measures.
why_wrong: A. Insect vectors transmit infections such as malaria and dengue, not acute gastroenteritis outbreaks. B. Blood-borne spread applies to hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. C. Sexual transmission does not explain a sudden group outbreak in a school party. D. Vertical spread occurs from mother to baby in pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.
pearl: Hepatitis A and typhoid are also spread by the faeco-oral route; food handlers with gastroenteritis should stay off work until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped.
thinking: Group outbreak of vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ No soap at the toilets ↓ Shared tap for drinking and washing up ↓ Contaminated hands, food and water ↓ Faeco-oral transmission
exam_trap: A, Mosquito-borne spread — camping outdoors makes insect bites seem relevant, but mosquitoes do not cause outbreaks of acute vomiting and diarrhoea.
takeaway: Outbreaks of gastroenteritis are usually spread by the faeco-oral route.
notes: Reviewer fix: pearl: reworded muddled link between hepatitis A/typhoid and the 48-hour food-handler exclusion

stem:
A 58-year-old man who moved to the UK from Pakistan two years ago is admitted with a month of night sweats, drenching fevers and marked weight loss. He takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. His chest X-ray shows countless tiny nodules scattered evenly through both lungs, liver enzymes are raised and fundoscopy reveals small pale choroidal lesions.

Which form of disease best accounts for this picture?
why_correct: Miliary tuberculosis results from haematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, seeding many organs at once. The diffuse 'millet seed' nodules on chest X-ray, abnormal liver tests and choroidal tubercles in an immunosuppressed man from a high-incidence country fit dissemination rather than localised lung disease. It is a medical emergency needing prompt specialist treatment.
why_wrong: A. Latent infection is asymptomatic and does not cause fever, weight loss or radiological lesions. B. Metastases are usually fewer, larger and of variable size, and would not explain choroidal tubercles. C. Sarcoidosis typically causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and is less likely with drenching fevers in this setting. D. Post-primary disease usually causes upper lobe cavitation rather than uniform tiny nodules in several organs.
pearl: Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are highly specific for miliary tuberculosis and can support the diagnosis before cultures return.
thinking: Immunosuppressed man from a high-incidence country ↓ Systemic symptoms with weight loss ↓ Uniform tiny nodules throughout both lungs ↓ Liver and eye involvement suggest blood-borne spread ↓ Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis
exam_trap: D, Cavitating post-primary tuberculosis — it is the commonest active form in adults, but cavitation is localised to the upper lobes and does not explain multi-organ seeding.
takeaway: Diffuse tiny lung nodules with involvement of other organs indicates haematogenous, miliary spread of tuberculosis.

stem:
Priya, aged 21, attends a sexual health clinic with burning on passing urine for five days. She also mentions a new yellowish vaginal discharge, some bleeding after intercourse and a dull ache low in her pelvis. She started a relationship with a new partner last month and they have not used condoms. She is afebrile and has no loin pain.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria accompanied by new abnormal discharge, post-coital bleeding and pelvic ache in a young woman with a recent new partner points to a sexually transmitted infection, and chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK. Cervicitis and urethritis can mimic cystitis, so a sexual history and vulvovaginal NAAT testing are needed rather than simply treating for a urinary infection.
why_wrong: A. A simple lower UTI does not explain new discharge or post-coital bleeding. B. Pyelonephritis would usually cause fever, loin pain and systemic upset. C. Bacterial vaginosis gives a thin, fishy-smelling discharge and does not usually cause dysuria, post-coital bleeding or pelvic pain. D. A stone presents with severe colicky loin-to-groin pain rather than discharge.
pearl: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so anyone tested for one STI should be offered testing for the others, and partners should be notified and treated.
thinking: Dysuria in a sexually active young woman ↓ New discharge and post-coital bleeding ↓ Recent new partner without condoms ↓ Afebrile, no loin pain ↓ Sexually transmitted infection, most likely chlamydia
exam_trap: A, Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection — dysuria draws attention to the bladder, but the discharge and post-coital bleeding point to cervicitis and an STI.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms plus new discharge or post-coital bleeding should prompt a sexual history and STI testing.

stem:
Over the past two days a 64-year-old retired teacher has become increasingly muddled and has been talking about smelling burning rubber. His wife brings him to the emergency department after he has a generalised seizure. He is febrile and drowsy, and MRI later shows signal change in the left temporal lobe.

Which drug should be given without delay?
why_correct: Fever, confusion, olfactory hallucinations, seizures and temporal lobe changes strongly suggest herpes simplex encephalitis. Intravenous aciclovir should be started as soon as encephalitis is suspected, without waiting for CSF PCR, because early treatment greatly reduces death and long-term disability.
why_wrong: B. Oral valaciclovir does not achieve reliable brain levels for acute encephalitis. C. Ganciclovir is used for cytomegalovirus, not first-line for herpes simplex. D. Steroids alone do not treat the viral infection. E. Oseltamivir treats influenza, not herpes simplex encephalitis.
pearl: Herpes simplex encephalitis has a predilection for the temporal lobes, which explains smell and taste hallucinations, memory loss and personality change.
thinking: Fever with acute confusion ↓ Olfactory hallucinations and seizure ↓ Temporal lobe involvement on imaging ↓ Suspected herpes simplex encephalitis ↓ Start intravenous aciclovir immediately
exam_trap: B, Oral valaciclovir — it is an effective antiherpes drug, but oral therapy is inadequate for a life-threatening CNS infection, which needs intravenous treatment.
takeaway: Suspected viral encephalitis is treated with intravenous aciclovir straight away, before confirmatory results.

stem:
In late summer, a 47-year-old forestry worker from the Scottish Highlands sees his GP because the left side of his face has drooped over the past day and he cannot close his left eye. About six weeks earlier he noticed a spreading red ring on his calf that faded on its own, and he has since had aching joints and fatigue. His forehead is also weak on the affected side.

Which infection is the most likely underlying cause?
why_correct: Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi from tick bites, can cause neurological involvement weeks after the initial rash, and facial nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy. An outdoor worker in a tick area with a previous expanding ring-shaped rash, arthralgia and lower motor neurone facial weakness fits early disseminated Lyme disease.
why_wrong: B. Herpes simplex type 2 causes genital lesions and occasionally meningitis, not this tick-linked picture. C. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms such as trismus, not flaccid facial palsy. D. Influenza does not typically cause an isolated facial nerve palsy weeks after a rash. E. Hepatitis A causes an acute hepatitis rather than cranial nerve palsy.
pearl: Facial palsy in Lyme disease can be bilateral, which is rare in idiopathic Bell's palsy and should prompt consideration of Lyme disease.
thinking: Outdoor worker in a tick-endemic area ↓ Previous expanding ring-shaped rash that faded ↓ Arthralgia and fatigue since ↓ Lower motor neurone facial palsy weeks later ↓ Early disseminated Lyme disease
exam_trap: B, Herpes simplex type 2 infection — herpes viruses are linked with facial palsy, but the preceding expanding rash and tick exposure point to Borrelia.
takeaway: Facial nerve palsy weeks after a tick bite or erythema migrans should prompt testing and treatment for Lyme disease.

stem:
A 71-year-old woman attends her GP practice with three days of severe burning pain deep in her right ear. Today her husband noticed that the right side of her face has dropped, she cannot wrinkle her right forehead and food tastes strange. On examination there are clusters of small blisters in the right external ear canal and on the pinna, and she reports ringing in that ear.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is reactivation of varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. It produces severe ear pain, a vesicular rash in the ear canal or pinna and an ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy, sometimes with taste disturbance, tinnitus, hearing loss or vertigo. The vesicles distinguish it from idiopathic Bell's palsy.
why_wrong: B. Bell's palsy causes facial weakness but no vesicles in the ear. C. Otitis externa causes canal pain and discharge but not facial nerve palsy. D. Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss without facial weakness or rash. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric shock-like facial pain without weakness or vesicles.
pearl: Ramsay Hunt syndrome has a worse prognosis for facial recovery than Bell's palsy; it is usually treated early with an oral antiviral plus prednisolone, with eye protection and prompt ENT input.
thinking: Severe ear pain ↓ Vesicles in the ear canal and pinna ↓ Ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness ↓ Taste change and tinnitus suggest geniculate ganglion involvement ↓ Ramsay Hunt syndrome
exam_trap: B, Idiopathic Bell's palsy — the facial weakness looks identical, but the ear vesicles indicate varicella zoster reactivation and change the treatment and prognosis.
takeaway: Facial palsy with vesicles in or around the ear is Ramsay Hunt syndrome, not Bell's palsy.
notes: Reviewer fix: 'calls into' changed to 'attends' (examination findings given); pearl now adds prompt ENT input.

stem:
A foundation doctor on a surgical ward is asked to take blood cultures from a 66-year-old man with rigors two days after a bowel resection. A senior nurse reminds her to clean the skin with chlorhexidine in alcohol, let it dry, avoid touching the site again and disinfect the bottle tops before inoculating them.

What is the main purpose of this careful technique?

options.A: To stop skin organisms entering the bloodstream and causing bacteraemia
options.B: To allow the samples to be taken after antibiotics have started
options.C: To avoid contaminating the sample and producing false-positive results
options.D: To improve the detection of fungal infection
options.E: To reduce the volume of blood needed in each bottle

correct_answer: C. To avoid contaminating the sample and producing false-positive results
why_correct: Skin commensals such as coagulase-negative staphylococci can easily enter the bottles if technique is poor, giving false-positive cultures. Contaminated results lead to unnecessary antibiotics, extra tests, longer stays and confusion about the true cause of sepsis, so aseptic non-touch technique protects the accuracy of the result.
why_wrong: A. Venepuncture rarely causes bacteraemia; the purpose of asepsis is the integrity of the sample. B. Cultures should ideally be taken before antibiotics whatever technique is used. D. Aseptic technique does not specifically improve fungal yield. E. Adequate filling of each bottle is still needed, as volume is a major factor in sensitivity.
pearl: The volume of blood cultured is one of the most important factors in sensitivity; underfilled bottles miss genuine bacteraemia.
thinking: Febrile post-operative patient needs cultures ↓ Skin flora can enter the sample ↓ Contaminants grow and look like true pathogens ↓ False positives drive unnecessary treatment ↓ Asepsis is about sample accuracy
exam_trap: A, Preventing bacteraemia — asepsis sounds like it protects the patient from infection, but its purpose in blood culture collection is to prevent contamination of the sample.
takeaway: Aseptic technique for blood cultures prevents contamination and misleading false-positive results.

stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a 10-hour history of severe headache, fever and neck stiffness. He is alert and orientated with no focal signs and no rash. Blood cultures have just been taken. The registrar wants a CT head before lumbar puncture, but the scanner is busy and nobody will be free to perform the lumbar puncture for at least an hour.

What should be done now?

options.B: Wait for the CT head, then perform lumbar puncture before antibiotics
options.C: Perform lumbar puncture first, then give antibiotics once CSF is obtained
options.D: Give oral amoxicillin and observe for a rash
options.E: Withhold antibiotics until the CSF Gram stain is reported

why_correct: In suspected bacterial meningitis, intravenous antibiotics should be given as soon as possible and must not be delayed by waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture. Blood cultures have already been taken, so the next step is empirical ceftriaxone; the lumbar puncture can still be performed later and CSF PCR remains useful after antibiotics.
why_wrong: B. Delaying antibiotics for a scan worsens outcome; the lumbar puncture can follow later. C. Lumbar puncture before antibiotics is only appropriate if it can be done promptly; here it cannot, so it must not hold up treatment. D. Oral therapy is inadequate for suspected bacterial meningitis. E. Waiting for the Gram stain causes a dangerous delay.
pearl: CSF PCR for meningococcus and pneumococcus can still give a diagnosis after antibiotics have started.
thinking: Fever, headache and neck stiffness ↓ Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Blood cultures already taken ↓ Investigations delayed ↓ Give intravenous antibiotics now
exam_trap: C, Lumbar puncture first — the wish for a diagnostic sample is understandable, but treatment delay increases death and neurological damage.
takeaway: Never let imaging or lumbar puncture delay antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem now states the LP cannot be done for at least an hour; without that, 'LP first then antibiotics' was defensible under NICE NG240 for an alert patient with no focal signs. why_wrong C reworded to match.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve has had low-grade fevers, night sweats and tiredness for three weeks. A new regurgitant murmur is heard, and she is haemodynamically stable with no signs of sepsis. The admitting team plans to take three sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites before starting antibiotics.

What is the main reason for this approach?

options.A: To give the best chance of identifying the causative organism
options.B: To measure the severity of the inflammatory response
options.D: To establish baseline renal function for antibiotic dosing
options.E: To confirm that she does not need valve surgery

correct_answer: A. To give the best chance of identifying the causative organism
why_correct: Endocarditis needs prolonged, targeted antibiotic treatment, so knowing the organism and its sensitivities is essential. Prior antibiotics are a leading cause of culture-negative endocarditis, and multiple sets from separate sites increase yield and help distinguish true continuous bacteraemia from contamination. In a stable patient this can be done without unsafe delay.
why_wrong: B. Inflammatory markers, not cultures, reflect the inflammatory response. C. Antibiotics do not alter echocardiographic findings in this way. D. Renal function is checked with blood tests, not cultures. E. Surgery decisions depend on echocardiography and clinical course, not on taking cultures.
pearl: Repeated positive cultures of a typical organism from separate sets is a major Duke criterion for infective endocarditis.
thinking: Prosthetic valve with fevers and new murmur ↓ Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Clinically stable, so a short wait is safe ↓ Antibiotics first reduce culture yield ↓ Several sets maximise organism identification
exam_trap: C, Preventing false-negative echocardiography — echocardiography is central to diagnosis, but antibiotics affect culture yield, not imaging.
takeaway: In stable suspected endocarditis, take multiple blood culture sets before antibiotics to identify the organism.

stem:
A 31-year-old man is seen in a medical admissions unit with two days of fever, extreme anxiety and episodes of throat spasm when he tries to drink water. Seven weeks ago, while volunteering in rural India, he was bitten on the hand by a stray dog and did not seek treatment. He now becomes agitated when a fan blows air at his face.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rabies is a lyssavirus infection transmitted by bites from infected mammals, particularly dogs in endemic regions. After an incubation of weeks to months it causes encephalitis with agitation, hydrophobia and aerophobia from pharyngeal spasm. Once symptoms appear it is almost always fatal, so post-exposure prophylaxis after any potential exposure is vital.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus causes trismus and muscle rigidity but not hydrophobia or aerophobia. B. Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis with clear consciousness. D. Viral meningitis causes headache and neck stiffness without throat spasm on drinking. E. Lyme disease follows tick bites and causes rash, arthralgia or cranial nerve palsy.
pearl: Any bite or scratch from a potentially rabid animal abroad needs prompt wound washing and urgent post-exposure assessment following UKHSA guidance, even weeks later.
thinking: Dog bite in a rabies-endemic country ↓ No post-exposure prophylaxis ↓ Weeks of incubation ↓ Agitation with spasm on drinking or air on the face ↓ Rabies encephalitis
exam_trap: A, Tetanus — it also follows wounds and causes spasms, but hydrophobia and aerophobia are characteristic of rabies.
takeaway: Hydrophobia and agitation weeks after an animal bite abroad suggest rabies.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman returned from visiting family in Nigeria ten days ago. She is brought to the emergency department with high fever, drowsiness and passing very little urine, and blood tests show acute kidney injury and a low glucose. A thick and thin blood film is sent.

Which species is most likely responsible for an illness this severe?
why_correct: Plasmodium falciparum is the predominant species in sub-Saharan Africa and causes most severe and fatal malaria. Infected red cells adhere to small vessels, leading to cerebral malaria, kidney injury, hypoglycaemia and acidosis. Reduced consciousness and organ dysfunction after travel to West Africa should be treated as severe falciparum malaria.
why_wrong: A. Vivax malaria can relapse but is less often severe and is uncommon in West Africa. B. Ovale malaria is usually milder and relapses from liver stages. D. Malariae causes a milder chronic infection, sometimes with nephrotic syndrome. E. Knowlesi can be severe but is acquired in South-East Asia, not Nigeria.
pearl: Severe falciparum malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, and the patient should be managed with specialist input.
thinking: Recent travel to sub-Saharan Africa ↓ Fever with reduced consciousness ↓ Kidney injury and hypoglycaemia ↓ Features of severe malaria ↓ Plasmodium falciparum
exam_trap: E, Plasmodium knowlesi — it can cause severe disease, but its geography (South-East Asia) does not fit travel to Nigeria.
takeaway: Severe malaria in a traveller from Africa is Plasmodium falciparum until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 27-year-old man is reviewed in an infectious diseases clinic having returned from Bangladesh three weeks ago. For over a week he has had a fever that climbs a little higher each day, a dull frontal headache, abdominal pain and constipation, now turning to loose stools. His pulse is slower than expected for his temperature, and a few faint rose-coloured spots are seen on his trunk. Three malaria films are negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Typhoid (enteric) fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread through food or water contaminated with faeces, and is common in South Asia. It typically gives a step-wise rising fever, headache, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea, relative bradycardia and rose spots. Blood cultures are the key investigation.
why_wrong: A. Giardiasis causes bloating and greasy diarrhoea with little fever. B. Norovirus causes short-lived vomiting and diarrhoea lasting a day or two. C. Hepatitis A causes jaundice and right upper quadrant pain rather than sustained fever with rose spots. E. Amoebic dysentery causes bloody diarrhoea and is not associated with relative bradycardia or rose spots.
pearl: Typhoid and paratyphoid are notifiable diseases in the UK, and many South Asian isolates are now resistant to fluoroquinolones.
thinking: Return from South Asia ↓ Step-wise rising fever over a week ↓ Abdominal pain with constipation then diarrhoea ↓ Relative bradycardia and rose spots ↓ Enteric fever
exam_trap: A, Giardiasis — it is a common travel-acquired infection, but it does not cause a sustained high fever, relative bradycardia or rose spots.
takeaway: Persistent fever with abdominal symptoms after travel to an area of poor sanitation should raise suspicion of typhoid.

stem:
Two weeks after returning from a holiday in the Caribbean, a 38-year-old man sees his GP with five days of fever, a widespread itchy red rash and severe pain and swelling in his wrists, fingers and ankles on both sides. He recalls many mosquito bites. He has had no diarrhoea, urethral discharge or new sexual partners, and no joint is hot and red.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Mosquito-borne viral arthritis such as chikungunya

correct_answer: B. Mosquito-borne viral arthritis such as chikungunya
why_correct: Fever, rash and acute symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints after mosquito exposure in the tropics is typical of an arboviral infection such as chikungunya. Joint pain can be severe and may persist for months. Dengue and Zika can look similar, and malaria should still be excluded when travel has been to an endemic area.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis usually affects one hot, swollen joint. C. Reactive arthritis follows gut or genital infection and is usually an asymmetrical large-joint oligoarthritis. D. Gout typically affects a single joint and does not cause a widespread rash with fever. E. Rheumatoid arthritis develops more gradually and is not accompanied by an acute febrile rash.
pearl: Chikungunya means 'that which bends up', describing the stooped posture caused by severe joint pain, which can persist for months.
thinking: Recent tropical travel with mosquito bites ↓ Fever and widespread rash ↓ Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis ↓ No gut or genital trigger ↓ Arboviral arthritis such as chikungunya
exam_trap: C, Reactive arthritis — joint symptoms after travel suggest it, but there was no preceding diarrhoea or genital infection and the pattern is symmetrical small-joint disease with a rash.
takeaway: Fever, rash and polyarthritis after tropical travel suggests a viral cause such as chikungunya.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman is found by paramedics at home with a fever and a stiff neck. In the emergency department her GCS is 10, her right pupil is larger than the left and she has weakness of her left arm. Bacterial meningitis is suspected and blood cultures have been taken.

Which investigation should not be performed at this stage?
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, a dilated pupil and focal limb weakness suggest raised intracranial pressure or a mass lesion, in which lumbar puncture risks brain herniation. Lumbar puncture should be delayed while intravenous antibiotics are given at once, and it may be reconsidered later once it is safe.
why_wrong: A. A chest X-ray can identify a pneumonia source and is safe. B. CT head is appropriate to look for a mass lesion or raised pressure, but must not delay antibiotics. C. Checking glucose is essential in any drowsy patient. E. Lactate helps assess sepsis severity.
pearl: Contraindications to early lumbar puncture include signs of raised intracranial pressure, shock, extensive purpura, coagulopathy and seizures that have not settled.
thinking: Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Low GCS with focal signs ↓ Possible raised intracranial pressure ↓ Lumbar puncture could cause herniation ↓ Defer lumbar puncture and give antibiotics now
exam_trap: B, CT head — scanning a drowsy patient can seem to waste time, but it is indicated here; it is the lumbar puncture that is unsafe.
takeaway: Focal signs or reduced consciousness in suspected meningitis mean deferring lumbar puncture, not antibiotics.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends her GP with five days of high temperatures, a painful throat, mouth ulcers and a faint blotchy rash over her trunk. She has tender nodes in the neck, axillae and groins. Three weeks ago she had condomless sex with a new partner she met abroad. A glandular fever screen is negative.

Which condition is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A flu-like or glandular-fever-like illness with rash, mouth ulcers and generalised lymphadenopathy two to four weeks after a sexual exposure is the typical picture of HIV seroconversion. A negative glandular fever screen makes EBV less likely. She should be offered a fourth-generation HIV test (antigen and antibody), which detects infection early; viral load is very high at this stage, so early diagnosis also reduces onward transmission.
why_wrong: A. Glandular fever is the main mimic, but the screen is negative and mouth ulcers with a truncal rash after a recent sexual exposure point to HIV. B. Streptococcal tonsillitis does not cause generalised lymphadenopathy with a rash and mucosal ulcers. C. Hodgkin lymphoma causes painless nodes developing over weeks to months, not an acute febrile illness. E. Sarcoidosis causes hilar nodes, erythema nodosum and arthralgia rather than a seroconversion illness.
pearl: BHIVA advises HIV testing in anyone with a glandular-fever-like illness, as primary HIV infection is frequently missed at first presentation.
thinking: Acute febrile illness with sore throat, mouth ulcers and rash ↓ Generalised lymphadenopathy ↓ Condomless sex with a new partner three weeks earlier ↓ Glandular fever screen negative ↓ Seroconversion illness: offer fourth-generation HIV test
exam_trap: A, Infectious mononucleosis — the sore throat and widespread nodes look like glandular fever, but a negative screen and recent sexual exposure should prompt an HIV test.
takeaway: Think of primary HIV infection in any glandular-fever-like illness after a recent sexual exposure, and test for it.

stem:
On the medical admissions unit, a 67-year-old woman is assessed for three weeks of night sweats, tiredness and weight loss. She had a dental extraction last month. There is a new pansystolic murmur and there are splinter haemorrhages in two fingernails. She is alert, warm and well perfused with a normal blood pressure, and has had no antibiotics. Infective endocarditis is suspected.

Which plan is most appropriate before antibiotics are given?

options.A: A single set of blood cultures taken from her existing cannula
options.B: Transthoracic echocardiogram, then antibiotics if vegetations are seen
options.C: Three sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites, spaced apart
options.D: Full blood count and C-reactive protein only
options.E: Midstream urine for microscopy and culture

correct_answer: C. Three sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites, spaced apart
why_correct: In a stable patient with suspected endocarditis, antibiotics can safely wait a short time while three sets of blood cultures are taken by separate venepunctures, ideally spaced apart. Bacteraemia in endocarditis is continuous, so several sets increase the yield and help distinguish a true pathogen from a skin contaminant. Identifying the organism and its sensitivities determines the long course of treatment.
why_wrong: A. One set drawn through an existing cannula has a high contamination rate and a lower yield. B. Echocardiography is important, but a normal transthoracic study does not exclude endocarditis and cultures should not depend on it. D. Inflammatory markers support the diagnosis but cannot identify the organism. E. A urine culture may be part of the wider work-up but does not replace blood cultures.
pearl: If the patient is septic or unstable, take two sets of blood cultures quickly and start empirical antibiotics without waiting.
thinking: Subacute fever, sweats and weight loss after dental work ↓ New murmur and splinter haemorrhages ↓ Haemodynamically stable and antibiotic-naive ↓ Organism identification guides prolonged therapy ↓ Three sets of cultures from separate sites before antibiotics
exam_trap: B, Echocardiogram first — imaging feels like the definitive test, but cultures must be taken before antibiotics and echocardiography cannot provide the organism or sensitivities.
takeaway: In stable suspected endocarditis, take three sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures before the first antibiotic dose.

stem:
A 63-year-old man is brought to the ED by his wife because he has become confused and drowsy over the course of the day. He has been treated for a painful left ear for a week. He is febrile, resists neck flexion and has no rash. After blood cultures and antibiotics, a lumbar puncture is done and the CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in the UK. Spread from a contiguous focus such as otitis media is a classic route, and pneumococci appear as Gram-positive diplococci on CSF microscopy. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a high mortality and risk of hearing loss, which is why dexamethasone is given alongside antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Listeria affects older or immunocompromised adults but appears as Gram-positive rods, not diplococci. B. Meningococci are Gram-negative diplococci and are more typical in younger people, often with a purpuric rash. D. Staphylococcus epidermidis causes shunt or device infections rather than community-acquired meningitis. E. Cryptococcus causes subacute meningitis in immunocompromised people and is seen on India ink staining, not as diplococci.
pearl: Recent otitis media, sinusitis, skull fracture with CSF leak, alcohol excess or splenectomy all raise the likelihood of pneumococcal meningitis.
thinking: Fever, confusion and neck stiffness in an older adult ↓ Preceding ear infection as a source ↓ CSF shows Gram-positive diplococci ↓ Commonest adult cause of bacterial meningitis ↓ Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_trap: B, Neisseria meningitidis — meningococcus is the best-known cause of meningitis, but it is a Gram-negative diplococcus and the ear source points to pneumococcus.
takeaway: In adults, especially with an ear or sinus source, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis.

stem:
At an urgent treatment centre, a 30-year-old woman who missed her childhood immunisations is seen with four days of fever, a runny nose, a hacking cough and sore red eyes. Today a blotchy red rash appeared at her hairline and is spreading down her body. Small white spots are seen on the inside of her cheeks.

Which option best describes the likely diagnosis and the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Rubella; reassure as no isolation is needed
options.C: Measles; move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
options.D: Drug eruption; stop any recent medicines and give an antihistamine
options.E: Parvovirus B19 infection; advise rest and fluids at home

correct_answer: C. Measles; move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
why_correct: A prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a rash starting at the hairline, with Koplik spots, is classical measles in an unimmunised adult. Measles is spread by the airborne route and is extremely infectious, so she must be isolated straight away, ideally in a single room with the door closed. Clinicians should then notify the local health protection team on clinical suspicion and arrange testing.
why_wrong: A. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue, not cough, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots. B. Rubella is milder, without a marked prodrome or Koplik spots, and the presentation here is measles. D. A drug eruption does not explain the coryzal prodrome and buccal spots. E. Parvovirus causes a slapped-cheek appearance and lacy rash, and sending her home without isolation ignores the infection risk.
pearl: Measles is infectious from about four days before to four days after the onset of the rash, and susceptible contacts may need post-exposure MMR or immunoglobulin.
thinking: Unimmunised adult ↓ Fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis ↓ Rash spreading downward from the hairline ↓ Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa ↓ Measles: isolate immediately, then notify
exam_trap: A, Scarlet fever — fever with a widespread red rash tempts a streptococcal diagnosis, but the respiratory prodrome, red eyes and Koplik spots are specific to measles.
takeaway: Suspected measles needs immediate airborne isolation and notification on clinical grounds, without waiting for results.

stem:
A 17-year-old girl is brought by ambulance from her school residential trip. Since the early hours she has had a high temperature, a pounding headache and aching legs, and her friends noticed purple spots on her ankles that do not fade when pressed. She is drowsy.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A rapidly evolving febrile illness with headache, limb pain and a non-blanching purpuric rash in a teenager is the classic picture of invasive meningococcal disease. Neisseria meningitidis carriage peaks in adolescents and young adults, especially in close-contact settings such as residential trips and halls. It can cause meningitis, septicaemia or both, and needs immediate antibiotics.
why_wrong: B. Listeria causes meningitis mainly in neonates, pregnant women, older people and the immunocompromised, without this purpuric rash. C. Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis, scarlet fever and cellulitis rather than meningitis with purpura. D. Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia and occasionally erythema multiforme, not purpura with sepsis. E. Escherichia coli is an important cause of neonatal meningitis, not of this picture in an adolescent.
pearl: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and abnormal skin colour are early signs of meningococcal sepsis that often precede the classic rash.
thinking: Teenager in a close-contact setting ↓ Hours-long febrile illness with headache and limb pain ↓ Non-blanching purpuric rash ↓ Drowsiness suggests evolving sepsis or meningitis ↓ Neisseria meningitidis
exam_trap: C, Streptococcus pyogenes — a febrile rash in a young person suggests streptococcal infection, but a non-blanching purpuric rash points to meningococcus.
takeaway: Fever with a non-blanching purpuric rash in an adolescent is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 45-year-old teacher contacts NHS 111 the day after returning from a school trip abroad. Since yesterday she has had frequent loose stools, crampy abdominal pain and a raised temperature. Several pupils from the same trip have developed identical symptoms.

Which broad category of illness is most likely?
why_correct: An acute illness with diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and fever, starting soon after travel and affecting several people who shared the same exposures, is an outbreak of infectious gastroenteritis until proven otherwise. Clustering is the key clue, since the alternatives are individual conditions. Food or water consumed during the trip is the likely source, and suspected outbreaks linked to food should be reported to public health.
why_wrong: A. Inflammatory bowel disease does not affect a group of people at the same time after shared exposure. C. Coeliac disease causes chronic symptoms related to gluten, not an acute febrile outbreak. D. Irritable bowel syndrome is chronic and does not cause fever. E. Ischaemic colitis affects older people with vascular disease and is not shared within a group.
pearl: Most travellers' diarrhoea is self-limiting; stool culture is indicated if there is blood, high fever, systemic illness or symptoms lasting more than about a week.
thinking: Acute diarrhoea, cramps and fever ↓ Onset right after travel ↓ Several people with the same exposure affected ↓ Clustering indicates an infectious source ↓ Infectious gastroenteritis
exam_trap: A, Inflammatory bowel disease — fever with diarrhoea and cramps can be an IBD flare, but a cluster among fellow travellers points to an infectious cause.
takeaway: Acute febrile diarrhoea affecting several people after a shared trip is infectious gastroenteritis.

presentation: Falciparum malaria in a returning traveller
stem:
A 58-year-old man attends the ED with his daughter, who says he has been getting drowsy and muddled since this morning. He came back 10 days ago from visiting relatives in Ghana and did not take any antimalarial tablets. For three days he has had high temperatures with shaking chills, and he now looks slightly jaundiced.

Which diagnosis must be excluded first?
why_correct: Fever in anyone who has returned from sub-Saharan Africa is falciparum malaria until proven otherwise, and confusion with jaundice suggests severe disease. People visiting friends and relatives often skip prophylaxis, which raises the risk. He needs urgent thick and thin blood films (or a rapid antigen test) and early specialist treatment, usually intravenous artesunate if severe.
why_wrong: A. Typhoid causes fever after travel but has a slower onset and is less immediately life-threatening, so malaria comes first. B. Dengue causes fever, headache and myalgia but is not the priority after travel to West Africa with confusion. C. Hepatitis A explains jaundice but not rigors with altered consciousness and is far less dangerous. E. Influenza does not explain jaundice and does not take priority over malaria in this traveller.
pearl: Falciparum malaria usually presents within a month of return, and one negative film does not exclude it; repeat films are needed over the following days if suspicion remains.
thinking: Returned from sub-Saharan Africa within the last month ↓ No chemoprophylaxis taken ↓ Fever with rigors ↓ Confusion and jaundice suggest severe disease ↓ Exclude falciparum malaria urgently
exam_trap: A, Typhoid fever — it is another serious cause of fever after travel, but falciparum malaria can kill within hours and must be excluded first.
takeaway: Any fever after travel to sub-Saharan Africa is falciparum malaria until blood films prove otherwise.

stem:
A GP reviews a 39-year-old man with a high temperature, sweats and headache for two days. He works for an engineering firm and has made several work trips overseas this year, some of them to tropical countries. The GP is considering malaria.

Which part of the history is most important to establish?

options.A: The airline and class of seat he flew in
options.B: Whether he has valid travel insurance
options.C: The exact places visited and the dates of each trip
options.D: The brand of sun cream he used
